ukladannya-granitnoyi-brukivky.title: Laying granite paving: technique and base
ukladannya-granitnoyi-brukivky.h1: How granite paving is laid — stages and base
ukladannya-granitnoyi-brukivky.description: Laying granite paving: base layers for a path and a driveway, slopes, kerbs, paving patterns, joint filling and care after laying.
ukladannya-granitnoyi-brukivky.dek: Base, slopes, joints and the order of work for a stable pavement.
ukladannya-granitnoyi-brukivky.intro: Granite paving lasts forever, but the base under it does not if it is done wrong. Sunken ruts on a driveway and “waves” on a path are always a mistake in the layers, compaction or water, never in the stone. We describe the technique we work by and explain how the base for pedestrians differs from the one for a car.

sections.heading: How to lay paving correctly?
sections.body:
The sequence is the same for every area: marking out and planning the slopes, excavating soil to the depth of all layers, geotextile, crushed stone compacted in layers, kerbs on concrete, a levelling layer, laying the stone, tamping, filling the joints.

The surface slope away from the building is at least 1.5–2 %, that is 2 cm per metre. Water must go to the lawn, a drainage channel or a gully, not to the wall. This rule is more important than the thickness of the stone.

sections.heading: What base to prepare?
sections.body:
Footpath: excavation 25–30 cm, geotextile, 20–40 mm crushed stone in a 15 cm layer compacted with a plate compactor, a levelling layer of granite screenings or a sand-cement mix 3–5 cm, paving 50–60 mm.

Driveway and parking space: excavation 40–45 cm, geotextile, 40–70 mm crushed stone in a 15 cm layer, 20–40 mm crushed stone in a 10 cm layer, each layer compacted separately, a levelling layer 3–4 cm, paving 80–100 mm. On weak soils a 10 cm layer of sand is added under the crushed stone, or a reinforced concrete slab.

Kerbs are set on a concrete bed before the stone is laid: they hold the pavement from spreading. Without kerbs, or with kerbs “on sand”, the edges sink in the first season.

sections.heading: What paving patterns are there?
sections.body:
In rows: the simplest and fastest, suits paths. Offset by half a sett: stronger, because the joints do not line up, the standard for driveways. In arcs and fans: the classic of European squares in split 100 × 100 mm setts; it needs experience and more stone, but carries loads excellently.

For contrasting patterns grey Grey Ukraine is combined with red Maple Red or black gabbro: borders, bands, a checkerboard module. Sawn-split setts with a flat top are more comfortable for walking in heels and cycling; fully split ones are more textured and work better on slopes.

sections.heading: How to care for it after laying?
sections.body:
For the first two weeks the joints are topped up: screenings or sand settle after rain and must be brought up to the level of the stone. After that, sweep once a year, top up the joints if needed and rinse with water. Polymer jointing sand holds better than ordinary sand and does not grow grass, but costs more.

In winter clear snow with a plastic or rubber shovel; salt does not harm granite. Moss on the shady north side is washed off with a pressure washer every few years. If one stone has sunk or is damaged, it is lifted, the base topped up and it is laid back: that is the main advantage of paving over asphalt and concrete.

rows: Only on top of compacted crushed stone
Layer-by-layer compaction with a plate compactor

faq.question: What paving thickness for a car?
faq.answer: 80–100 mm for passenger cars and 100 mm for lorries. Footpaths — 50–60 mm.

faq.question: Is concrete needed?
faq.answer: Under the paving itself usually not: compacted crushed stone and screenings work better because they let water through. Concrete is needed under kerbs and channels and on weak or fill soils.

faq.question: How to fill the joints?
faq.answer: With granite screenings or fine sand, swept into the joints and watered in several passes. Polymer sand holds longer and does not grow weeds.

faq.question: How long does it last?
faq.answer: The stone — indefinitely. The base with correct technique — 30 years and more without relaying.

kamin-dlya-kaminu-granit-marmur.title: Stone for a fireplace: granite, marble or travertine
kamin-dlya-kaminu-granit-marmur.h1: Which stone to choose for fireplace cladding
kamin-dlya-kaminu-granit-marmur.description: Stone for a fireplace: granite, marble, travertine or labradorite. Heat resistance, technical gaps from the firebox, adhesive, care and the look of the surround.
kamin-dlya-kaminu-granit-marmur.dek: The stone and cladding detail for different types of fireplace.
kamin-dlya-kaminu-granit-marmur.intro: A fireplace surround is the most visible stone piece in a living room, and it works in the harshest conditions: heat, soot, sharp temperature changes. Natural stone was made for this, but the rock, the detail and the adhesive must match the type of fireplace. We explain the difference between wood-burning, gas and electric and what we advise for each.

sections.heading: Which stone suits a fireplace?
sections.body:
For a wood-burning fireplace with an open or closed firebox: granite or gabbro for the surround and especially for the hearth in front of the firebox, where sparks and embers fall. For gas: any stone, including marble, because the heating is moderate. For electric: no restrictions, it is furniture.

Volga Blue labradorite is one of the most striking options for a surround: the blue flash of the crystals comes alive in firelight. Travertine is chosen for warm Mediterranean interiors, but its pores need protection from soot.

sections.heading: Why is granite better for active use?
sections.body:
Granite does not change colour when heated to 200–250 °C, does not absorb soot once sealed, withstands knocks from logs and washes easily. On the hearth in front of the firebox it can be cleaned of embers with a stiff brush. A polished surface reflects the fire and adds light to the room.

Granite's thermal expansion is small, but the surround is not glued tight to the firebox: a 5–10 mm gap with heat-resistant sealant or mineral wool is left between metal and stone, and the slabs are laid on heat-resistant stone adhesive.

sections.heading: When to choose marble?
sections.body:
Marble is the classic of fireplace surrounds from Versailles to Lviv townhouses. Choose it for gas and electric fireplaces or for wood-burning ones with a closed firebox, where the surround does not touch the flame and has a technical gap.

Soot and fingerprints show on marble, and acidic cleaners for the firebox glass etch the surface. So a marble surround is cared for only with neutral products and sealed once a year. Bianco Carrara and Nero Marquina are the most common choice; Crema Marfil gives a warm calm surround for a light living room.

sections.heading: What about heat resistance and care?
sections.body:
Natural stone withstands the heat a surround reaches, but not sudden local heating: a hot cast-iron pot on a marble hearth can leave a mark or a crack. That is why we make the hearth in front of a wood-burning firebox from granite or gabbro.

Care: soot is washed off with water and a neutral cleaner, heavy dirt with a baking soda poultice. Granite is sealed every two to three years, marble and travertine every year. Once a season inspect the gap between the firebox and the stone: the sealant must be elastic and free of cracks.

faq.question: Does marble take the heat?
faq.answer: Moderate heating of the surround — yes. Direct contact with flame, sparks or hot metal — no; for those zones we use granite.

faq.question: What for a wood-burning fireplace?
faq.answer: Granite or gabbro for the surround and hearth, heat-resistant adhesive, a 5–10 mm gap from the firebox with elastic sealant.

faq.question: What for a classic look?
faq.answer: Bianco Carrara or Nero Marquina marble with a profiled edge, sometimes with carved elements. For a gas or closed firebox it is a safe choice.

faq.question: How to clean the surround?
faq.answer: With a neutral stone cleaner and a soft cloth. Soot with a baking soda poultice. No acids, especially on marble, and no firebox glass cleaners on the stone.

landshaftnyy-kamin-dvir.title: Landscape stone for a yard: types and uses
landshaftnyy-kamin-dvir.h1: Landscape stone — how to choose it for a yard and garden
landshaftnyy-kamin-dvir.description: Landscape stone for a yard: slabs for paths, retaining walls, kerbs, flower beds. Frost resistance, slip-resistant finish, combining with paving and the facade.
landshaftnyy-kamin-dvir.dek: Stone for paths, flower beds, retaining walls and decorative zones.
landshaftnyy-kamin-dvir.intro: In a garden stone works differently than in a house: there are no hot pans here, but there is frost, water, roots and a lawnmower. Landscape stone is chosen not for its beauty on the slab but for its function: what to walk on, what to hold, what to highlight. We explain which granite products we make for yards and how they combine with paving and the facade.

sections.heading: Which landscape stone to choose?
sections.body:
Granite covers every task in a yard: slabs for paths and terraces, kerbs, steps, retaining walls, cladding for flower beds and ponds. It is frost-resistant, unafraid of water and salt, and a flamed surface is not slippery. Sandstone and limestone are softer and more porous; in our climate they flake after a few winters.

For decorative zones split stone from production offcuts suits well: rubble for dry walls, cobbles for flower beds. It is an affordable way to get a natural texture, and we offer it together with the main products.

sections.heading: Which types are used in a yard?
sections.body:
Slabs for paths and terraces: 30–40 mm for laying on crushed stone and sand, 20 mm on a concrete base, formats from 300 × 300 to 600 × 900 mm, flamed or sawn finish. Steps and garden stairs: solid blocks or 30–40 mm overlay treads on concrete.

Retaining walls: granite blocks 200–400 mm or cladding slabs on a concrete core. Kerbs: sawn or split, 80–150 mm high, holding paths and the lawn. Cladding: flower beds, bowls, ponds, outdoor kitchens, benches and barbecue tops of flamed granite.

sections.heading: How to combine stone with paving and the facade?
sections.body:
One rule: no more than two stones in a yard. For example, Grey Ukraine in the paving and terrace slabs plus Kometa Black in kerbs, steps and accent bands. If the facade or plinth is stone, the landscaping continues its stone.

Match finishes to function: polished only on verticals and accents, flamed everywhere people walk. Module sizes should be matched in multiples to the paving (100 mm) so a slab path and a paved driveway meet without trimming.

sections.heading: How to care for landscape stone?
sections.body:
Twice a year rinse with a pressure washer, especially shaded areas where moss grows. Sealing is not needed for granite outdoors; for sandstone and limestone a water repellent every few years.

In winter a plastic shovel and any de-icer; granite tolerates them. Once a year check the joints between slabs and kerbs and top up if needed. Plant trees with aggressive roots (willow, poplar, bamboo) no closer than 2–3 m from paths: roots lift slabs regardless of the type of stone.

faq.question: Which stone is frost-resistant?
faq.answer: Granite, gabbro and labradorite: water absorption below 0.2 %, over 300 freeze cycles without change. Sandstone and limestone flake in our climate.

faq.question: Is it slippery after rain?
faq.answer: Polished — yes, which is why we do not lay it outdoors. Flamed, bush-hammered and sawn granite are slip-resistant when wet.

faq.question: How to lay it?
faq.answer: 30–40 mm slabs on compacted crushed stone and screenings like paving, 20 mm on concrete and adhesive. Kerbs and steps on a concrete bed.

faq.question: How to clean it?
faq.answer: With a pressure washer twice a year. Moss washes off, salt does not harm granite, sealing is not needed.

skilky-koshtue-stilnytsia-z-kamenyu.title: How much does a stone countertop cost: what the price depends on
skilky-koshtue-stilnytsia-z-kamenyu.h1: What the cost of a stone countertop depends on
skilky-koshtue-stilnytsia-z-kamenyu.description: The cost of a stone countertop: material, area and cutting, thickness, edge, cut-outs, reinforcement, delivery and installation. How to get an exact estimate.
skilky-koshtue-stilnytsia-z-kamenyu.dek: The factors of the estimate without misleading universal prices.
skilky-koshtue-stilnytsia-z-kamenyu.intro: “How much does a stone countertop cost per metre?” is the most common question, and there is no honest short answer. Two countertops of the same length in the same stone can differ in price twofold because of cutting, cut-outs and the edge. We explain what the estimate consists of, in what order the factors affect the sum and how to get an exact figure within a day.

sections.heading: How much does a stone countertop cost?
sections.body:
The estimate consists of four parts: material (a slab or part of it), fabrication (cutting, edge, cut-outs, polishing of edges), extra elements (splashback, reinforcement, laminated edge) and logistics with installation.

Material usually makes up 40 to 60 % of the sum, fabrication 25–40 %, the rest is delivery and installation. That is why the question “per metre” misleads: a price per linear metre of stone ignores half the work. A guide for specific dimensions is given by the calculator on the site; it works by exactly this logic.

sections.heading: Which factors affect the price?
sections.body:
Material: stone, brand, rarity of colour. Area and cutting: we pay for the whole slab, so it matters how many slabs are needed and how the parts fit on them; a 3.1 m countertop may need two slabs instead of one.

Thickness: 30 mm is more expensive than 20 mm in both material and fabrication. Edge: a straight edge is basic, bevel and rounding slightly more, ogee, waterfall and a 40–60 mm laminated edge considerably more. Cut-outs: every cut-out for a sink, hob, tap or socket adds work, and an undermount sink needs the inner perimeter polished.

Installation: floor, lift, length of parts, joints on site, reinforcement of overhangs. A countertop for the fifth floor without a lift costs more than the same one on the ground floor.

sections.heading: How does the material affect the cost?
sections.body:
Roughly, the catalogue materials fall into three tiers. Base: Ukrainian granites Grey Ukraine, Maple Red, Rosso Santiago and porcelain in standard decors. Mid: gabbro, labradorite, branded Vicostone and Caesarstone quartz from the base collections. Premium: marble, Taj Mahal quartzite, Calacatta-look quartz collections, Dekton and Neolith.

Within one tier the price difference is small, between tiers it is noticeable. One more nuance: light uniform materials are usually more expensive than dark patterned ones, because they are harder to produce without flaws. The “from” prices for each collection are shown on its catalogue page.

sections.heading: How to get an exact estimate quickly?
sections.body:
Step one: the calculator on the site with dimensions, product type and material gives a guide within a minute. Step two: send us the kitchen plan or a photo with dimensions, and we calculate the cutting and the full estimate within a day. Step three: measurement on site after the furniture is installed fixes the final sum, which no longer changes.

To avoid overpaying, think about three things before the measurement: whether a laminated edge is needed, whether the joint can be moved to where it is not visible, and whether a stone splashback is needed along the whole length or only behind the hob.

rows: Stone tier and number of slabs
Length over 3 m = a second slab
Laminated edge and undermount sink cost more

faq.question: Which is more expensive — granite or quartz?
faq.answer: Ukrainian granites are usually more affordable than branded quartz. Imported granite in rare colours and premium quartz collections cost about the same.

faq.question: Is installation included?
faq.answer: In the estimate installation is a separate line, as is delivery. This lets you see what you pay for and, if you wish, order fabrication only.

faq.question: How to calculate it myself?
faq.answer: The calculator on the site works from dimensions, product type, material, edge and number of cut-outs. It is a guide with an accuracy of about ±15 %; the cutting layout refines the rest.

faq.question: What affects it most?
faq.answer: Material and the number of slabs. Then edge and cut-outs. 30 mm thickness instead of 20 mm adds 20–40 %.

shcho-take-slyab.title: What a slab is and where it is used
shcho-take-slyab.h1: Slab — what it is, sizes and uses
shcho-take-slyab.description: A slab is a large sheet of natural or engineered stone. Slab sizes for granite, marble, quartz and porcelain, thickness, how to choose and what a remnant is.
shcho-take-slyab.dek: How to read the whole sheet, batch, tone and usable area.
shcho-take-slyab.intro: A slab is a large sheet of stone sawn from a block and polished on one side. It is from slabs that countertops, window sills, stairs and cladding are cut, and it is the slab, not a 10 × 10 cm sample, that you need to look at before ordering. We explain what kinds of slabs there are, their sizes and how your countertop comes out of them.

sections.heading: What is a slab?
sections.body:
At the quarry stone is extracted in blocks weighing 10–30 tonnes. The block is sawn into sheets 20 or 30 mm thick on wire or disc saws, then the face is ground and polished. The finished sheet is the slab: in natural stone the size is set by the block, in quartz and porcelain by the factory format.

Every slab has a number, a batch and actual dimensions, and natural stones also an individual pattern. That is why in the catalogue we show not “grey granite” but specific slabs with photos, dimensions and availability status.

sections.heading: What kinds of granite, marble and quartzite slabs are there?
sections.body:
Granite: the largest group, Ukrainian and imported, 20 and 30 mm thick, polished, honed, flamed or leather finish. Marble: imported from Italy, Spain, Turkey, 20 and 30 mm thick, often with a reinforcing mesh on the back because of brittleness. Quartzite: Brazil and India, 20 and 30 mm thick, the hardest and most expensive of the natural stones.

Quartz (engineered): factory sheets of standard format, 20 and 30 mm thick, uniform colour. Porcelain: 6, 12 and 20 mm, format up to 3200 × 1600 mm, with a decor only on the surface or through-body depending on the collection.

sections.heading: What standard sizes does a slab have?
sections.body:
Granite and marble: from 2400 × 1200 to 3200 × 1900 mm, most often about 2800 × 1600 mm. The size depends on the block and the stone: Ukrainian granites are usually 2400–3000 × 1200–1500 mm. Quartz: standard 3050 × 1400 mm, Jumbo format 3200 × 1600 mm in premium collections.

Porcelain: Laminam 3240 × 1620 mm, Neolith 3200 × 1600 mm, Dekton 3200 × 1440 mm. The usable area is always smaller than the overall size: the edges of the sheet have a 20–50 mm margin with sawing defects, and natural stone may have cracks or inclusions that we avoid when cutting.

sections.heading: Where are slabs used?
sections.body:
Countertops and islands: from granite, quartz, quartzite and porcelain. Window sills and stairs: from granite, marble. Cladding of walls, fireplaces and facades: from any stone in large-format sheets when a “seamless” pattern or bookmatch, the mirror pairing of two adjacent slabs, is wanted.

Slab remnants after cutting are a separate category: 0.5–1.5 m pieces that become window sills, small tables, shelves and small countertops at a lower price. Ours are available on the remnants page with dimensions and photos.

rows: Often with mesh on the back

faq.question: How does a slab differ from a tile?
faq.answer: In size and in what is made from it. A tile is a finished module up to 1200 mm to be laid on adhesive. A slab is a blank up to 3.2 m from which the piece is cut to your size.

faq.question: What sizes does a slab have?
faq.answer: Natural stone from 2.4 × 1.2 to 3.2 × 1.9 m, quartz 3.05 × 1.4 or 3.2 × 1.6 m, porcelain 3.2 × 1.6 m. Exact dimensions are given for each sheet in the catalogue.

faq.question: How much does it cost?
faq.answer: A slab is sold per square metre with a factor for the whole sheet. The price depends on the stone, thickness and batch; the catalogue shows the price of specific slabs in stock.

faq.question: How to choose a slab?
faq.answer: Look at the whole sheet in daylight, not a sample: check the pattern, cracks, inclusions, agree the layout of the parts on the sheet. We send photos and video of the slab and hold it for you until cutting.

yak-vybraty-kamin-dlya-kukhni.title: How to choose stone for a kitchen: the complete 2026 guide
yak-vybraty-kamin-dlya-kukhni.h1: How to choose stone for a kitchen countertop — the complete guide
yak-vybraty-kamin-dlya-kukhni.description: How to choose stone for a kitchen: granite, quartz, quartzite, porcelain or marble. Comparison by strength, heat, care, pattern and budget, thickness and edge.
yak-vybraty-kamin-dlya-kukhni.dek: The main guide by strength, heat, care and the character of the pattern.
yak-vybraty-kamin-dlya-kukhni.intro: Choosing stone for a kitchen starts not with the name of the material but with three questions: how you cook, how much attention you are willing to give to care, and what character the kitchen should have. Answer them and you almost automatically get one of five materials. In this guide we have gathered everything we explain to clients at the workshop, with links to the detailed articles.

sections.heading: Which stone to choose for a kitchen?
sections.body:
You cook a lot, put hot things wherever, love a natural pattern: granite. You want a light uniform surface and minimal care, hot things on a trivet: quartz. You want a light natural stone with veins that is not afraid of lemon: quartzite. You need a thin modern countertop you can put hot things on: porcelain. You are ready for patina for the sake of beautiful marble: marble, but understanding the consequences.

It is a simplified scheme, but it works in most cases. Now the nuances.

sections.heading: Granite, quartz, quartzite, porcelain or marble — what is the difference?
sections.body:
Granite: natural rock, hardness 6–7, takes heat, needs sealing every 1–3 years, every slab unique, Ukrainian stones affordable.

Quartz: 90 % quartz with resin, no pores, repeatable colour, sensitive to temperatures above 150 °C and to ultraviolet, not for outdoors.

Quartzite: natural, hardness 7, acid-resistant, needs sealing, light warm tones, the most expensive of the natural stones.

Porcelain: a sintered 12 mm sheet, afraid of nothing except a blow to the edge, the lightest, needs a continuous substrate and a bevelled edge.

Marble: calcite, hardness 3–4, etched by acids, the most beautiful pattern, for a kitchen with a careful owner or for an island where no cooking is done.

sections.heading: What to consider for strength, care and budget?
sections.body:
Impact and scratch resistance: quartzite and granite, then quartz and porcelain (brittle edges), then marble. Stain resistance without sealing: quartz and porcelain, then quartzite and granite with sealing, then marble.

Care: quartz and porcelain nothing but washing; granite and quartzite a water test and sealing; marble sealing every year and always neutral chemistry. Budget in ascending order: Ukrainian granites and basic porcelain, then quartz and gabbro, then marble, quartzite and premium collections of quartz and porcelain.

sections.heading: What thickness and finish are needed?
sections.body:
Thickness: 20 mm for a standard kitchen in all materials, 30 mm for long consoles or a massive style, 12 mm for porcelain with a laminated edge. Edge: straight or bevel as standard, R3 rounding for families with children, a 40 mm laminated edge for the look of a thick slab.

Finish: polished shows the pattern and is easier to wash; honed hides fingerprints and etching on marble; leather on dark granite adds tactility and hides scratches. In a kitchen with a south-facing window dark polished stone will give glare — keep that in mind.

sections.heading: How to order and calculate the cost?
sections.body:
Get a guide price in the calculator, pick two or three collections in the catalogue and write to us with the kitchen plan. We will send photos of the slabs in stock, an estimate with the cutting layout and a measurement date. After the measurement you approve the layout of the parts on the specific slab, and within one to two weeks the countertop is in the kitchen.

If you are torn between two materials, come to the workshop in Kostopil or order samples: you can run a home test on them with lemon, a hot cup and a knife, after which the choice becomes obvious.

rows: Trivet for hot things, not for outdoors

faq.question: What is the most practical?
faq.answer: Quartz for a light kitchen, granite for any other. Both forgive daily use; the difference is only in hot pans and sealing.

faq.question: What to choose for a family with children?
faq.answer: Quartz or granite with a rounded R3 edge. Porcelain takes knocks from toys on the edge worse, and marble needs attention that a family with children usually does not have.

faq.question: What needs sealing?
faq.answer: Granite, quartzite and marble. Quartz and porcelain have no pores and are not sealed.

faq.question: Where to start the choice?
faq.answer: With the scenario: how you cook and how much care you are willing to give. Then with the colour and pattern in the catalogue, then with the calculator and samples.
